items.question: The melting point of ice is:
items.explanation: Melting point of ice = 0degrees C = 273 K (0 + 273 = 273 K). This is the temperature at which solid ice converts to liquid water. Boiling point of water = 100degrees C = 373 K.

items.question: Solid CO2 is called dry ice because:

options.A: It is used for drying clothes
options.B: It is very cold and dry to touch
options.C: It converts directly from solid to gas without forming liquid, so no wetness/liquid is formed
options.D: It is made from dry gas

items.explanation: Solid CO2 sublimes directly from solid to gas at normal atmospheric pressure without passing through the liquid state. Since no liquid is formed, it is called "dry" ice. It looks like ice but leaves no liquid behind.

items.question: During the change of state from solid to liquid, the temperature:

options.C: Remains constant at the melting point

items.explanation: Temperature remains constant at the melting point during melting because the supplied heat (latent heat of fusion) is used to overcome inter-particle forces (change state), not to raise temperature.

items.question: Why does steam at 100degrees C cause more severe burns than boiling water at 100degrees C?

options.C: Steam particles have absorbed extra energy (latent heat of vaporisation) which is released on skin causing more severe burns
options.D: Boiling water is cooler than steam

items.explanation: Steam particles at 373 K have absorbed latent heat of vaporisation in addition to the heat content of water at 373 K. When steam condenses on skin, it releases this extra latent heat energy, causing more severe burns than boiling water at the same temperature.

items.question: Convert 573 K to Celsius.
items.explanation: degrees C = K - 273 = 573 - 273 = 300degrees C.

options.B: Sublimation - direct conversion of solid to gas without liquid state

items.explanation: Naphthalene undergoes sublimation - it converts directly from solid to vapour/gas state without forming any liquid. Hence no liquid residue is found. The solid just seems to disappear. This is the same as camphor balls disappearing.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: When heat is supplied to a substance, the kinetic energy of its particles increases. This can cause the substance to change its state - from solid to liquid (melting) at the melting point, and from liquid to gas (boiling) at the boiling point.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: MELTING POINT: Minimum temperature at which solid melts to liquid at atmospheric pressure.
Melting point of ice = 273.15 K (0degrees C). For convenience = 273 K.
LATENT HEAT OF FUSION: Heat to change 1 kg solid to liquid at melting point. Hidden heat - does not raise temperature.
Temperature stays constant during melting and boiling.
Particles in water (273 K) have MORE energy than particles in ice (273 K) - they absorbed latent heat.
BOILING POINT: Temperature at which liquid boils at atmospheric pressure.
Boiling point of water = 373 K (100degrees C). 100degrees C = 273 + 100 = 373 K.
BOILING: Bulk phenomenon - particles from the entire bulk of liquid change to vapour.
LATENT HEAT OF VAPORISATION: Heat to change 1 kg liquid to gas at boiling point.
Particles in steam (373 K) have MORE energy than particles in water (373 K) - steam burns more.
Melting point of a solid = indication of strength of inter-particle force.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.12:
sections.aim: To study the effect of heat on change of state of water and to find melting and boiling points.
sections.materials: 150 g of ice, laboratory thermometer, beaker, iron stand, glass stirrer, burner.
procedure: - Take 150 g of ice in a beaker. Suspend thermometer with bulb in ice.
- Start heating on low flame. Note temperature when ice starts melting.
- Note temperature when all ice converts to water.
- Put glass rod; heat till water boils. Keep careful eye on thermometer till most water vaporises.
sections.observation:
- Ice melts at 0degrees C (273 K). Temperature stays at 0degrees C till all ice melts.
- Water boils at 100degrees C (373 K). Temperature stays at 100degrees C till all water vaporises.
sections.conclusion: Melting point of ice = 273 K. Boiling point of water = 373 K. Temperature remains constant during change of state (latent heat is absorbed).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.13 - Sublimation of Camphor:
sections.materials: Camphor, china dish, inverted funnel, cotton plug, burner.
procedure: - Crush camphor and put in china dish. Put inverted funnel over dish. Put cotton plug on stem of funnel. Heat slowly and observe.
sections.observation: Camphor vapours rise. White solid camphor appears on cooler inner surface of funnel stem.
sections.conclusion:
Camphor changes directly from solid to gas (sublimation) and back to solid (deposition) without passing through liquid state.

items.question: What is latent heat of vaporisation? How is it different from latent heat of fusion?
items.answer:
LATENT HEAT OF VAPORISATION: The heat energy required to change 1 kg of liquid into gas at atmospheric pressure at its boiling point. This heat is "hidden" - it does not raise the temperature; it overcomes inter-particle forces in liquid.
LATENT HEAT OF FUSION: The heat energy required to change 1 kg of solid into liquid at atmospheric pressure at its melting point.
DIFFERENCE: Latent heat of fusion is absorbed during solid->liquid change at melting point. Latent heat of vaporisation is absorbed during liquid->gas change at boiling point. Both are "hidden" (latent) because they do not cause temperature rise.

items.question: Why is ice at 273 K more effective in cooling than water at 273 K?
items.answer:
Both ice and water are at 273 K (same temperature). However:
ICE: When ice is used to cool something, it first absorbs LATENT HEAT OF FUSION (336 J/g approximately) to melt from solid to liquid without any temperature rise. After melting, the resulting water absorbs further heat to warm up.
WATER at 273 K: Can only absorb heat to warm up (no phase change, no latent heat involved).
CONCLUSION: Ice absorbs much more total heat from surroundings (latent heat of fusion + warming up heat) than water at the same temperature. Therefore, ice at 273 K is MORE EFFECTIVE in cooling than water at 273 K.

items.question: Describe Activity 1.13 (sublimation of camphor). What does it prove?

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.13 - Sublimation of Camphor:
sections.materials: Camphor crystals, china dish, inverted funnel, cotton plug, burner.
procedure: Step 1: Take some camphor. Crush it and put it in a china dish.
Step 2: Put an inverted funnel over the china dish.
Step 3: Put a cotton plug on the stem of the funnel to prevent vapours from escaping.
Step 4: Heat the china dish slowly on a burner and observe.
sections.observation:
- Camphor is heated -> camphor vapours (gas) rise upward through the funnel.
- The vapours cool as they go up in the funnel.
- White solid camphor particles form (solidify) on the cooler inner surface of the funnel stem.
- No liquid camphor is observed at any stage.
sections.conclusion:
Temperature change causes change of state. Latent heat is absorbed during melting (at melting point) and boiling (at boiling point) without raising temperature. The heat is used to overcome inter-particle forces to change the state of matter.

items.question: The SI unit of temperature is:
items.explanation: Kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature. 0degrees C = 273 K. To convert: K = degrees C + 273. The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero (-273degrees C).

items.question: Boiling point of water is:
items.explanation: Boiling point of water = 100degrees C = 373 K (100 + 273 = 373 K). Melting point of ice = 0degrees C = 273 K.

items.question: Why does temperature remain constant at 0degrees C while ice is melting?

options.B: Heat supplied is used to overcome inter-particle forces (latent heat of fusion) not to raise temperature
options.C: Ice absorbs no heat during melting

items.explanation: During melting, all heat supplied is used as latent heat of fusion to overcome the inter-particle forces in ice and change it to liquid. None of the heat increases kinetic energy (temperature). Temperature remains constant at 0degrees C until all ice melts.

items.question: Particles in steam at 373 K have _______ energy than particles in water at 373 K.
items.explanation: Steam particles at 373 K have absorbed the latent heat of vaporisation in addition to the heat content of water. Therefore, steam particles have more energy than water particles at the same temperature (373 K). This explains why steam burns are more severe.

items.question: In Activity 1.13, camphor vapours that rise and solidify on the funnel surface is an example of:
items.explanation: In Activity 1.13, camphor first sublimes (solid->gas) when heated, then the vapours solidify directly on the cooler funnel surface (gas->solid) without forming any liquid. This direct gas to solid conversion is called deposition.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The state of matter can also be changed by changing pressure without necessarily changing temperature. Applying pressure brings gas particles closer together, which can convert gas to liquid (liquefaction). The state of a substance is determined by both temperature AND pressure together.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The difference between states is due to difference in distances between constituent particles.
Applying pressure brings particles closer -> state can change.
LIQUEFACTION: Converting gas to liquid by applying pressure and reducing temperature.
DRY ICE: Solid CO2 stored under high pressure. At 1 atmosphere, it sublimes directly (solid->gas) without forming liquid CO2.
Pressure and temperature TOGETHER determine the state of a substance.
Applying pressure + reducing temperature = effective method to liquefy gases.
LPG is liquefied and stored in cylinders under high pressure.

items.question: How can a gas be liquefied? What two conditions are required?
items.answer:
A gas can be liquefied (converted to liquid) by:
(1) APPLYING HIGH PRESSURE: By applying pressure, gas particles are forced closer together, reducing the distance between them. This helps bring them close enough for inter-particle forces to act.
(2) REDUCING TEMPERATURE: By reducing temperature, kinetic energy of particles decreases. With less kinetic energy, particles cannot escape inter-particle forces and stay together as liquid.
Both conditions together effectively liquefy gases. Example: LPG is liquefied by applying high pressure and stored in cooking cylinders.

items.question: Explain why solid CO2 is called dry ice. What happens to it at normal atmospheric pressure?
items.answer:
SOLID CO2 AND DRY ICE:
Solid carbon dioxide (CO2) is called DRY ICE because it converts directly from solid to gas (sublimes) without forming any liquid at normal atmospheric pressure.

WHAT HAPPENS:
At HIGH PRESSURE: CO2 remains as solid (solid CO2 = dry ice). It is stored in this form.
At NORMAL ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE (1 atmosphere):
- Solid CO2 does NOT melt to form liquid CO2.
- Instead, it undergoes SUBLIMATION - converts directly from solid to gaseous state.
- No liquid is formed at any stage.
- The solid simply disappears as gas, leaving no liquid residue.

WHY "DRY":
Ordinary ice (solid water) melts to form liquid water when warmed - it is "wet."
Solid CO2 does not form any liquid - it goes directly to gas. No wetness or liquid is formed. Hence it is called "DRY" ice.

PRACTICAL USE: Dry ice is used in cold storage and transport of food and medicines because:
(1) It is colder than ordinary ice.
(2) It does not leave any liquid mess (goes directly to gas).
(3) The CO2 gas also creates a preservative atmosphere.

items.question: How does pressure determine the state of matter? Explain with examples and the relationship between pressure, temperature, and state of matter.
items.answer:
PRESSURE AND STATE OF MATTER:

The state of matter depends on both temperature and pressure together. Pressure can change the state of matter even without changing temperature significantly.

HOW PRESSURE CHANGES STATE:

GAS TO LIQUID (by increasing pressure):
When pressure is applied on a gas, the particles are forced closer together. The distance between particles decreases. When particles come close enough, inter-particle forces become significant. Combined with reduced temperature, the gas liquefies.
Example: Oxygen gas is stored as liquid oxygen in high-pressure cylinders for hospitals.

LIQUID TO GAS (by decreasing pressure):
When pressure on a liquid is reduced, particles can move further apart. At low enough pressure, even a liquid can convert to gas.
Example: Water boils at lower temperature at high altitudes (less atmospheric pressure) - like on mountains.

SOLID TO GAS (by decreasing pressure):
Solid CO2 (dry ice) at high pressure remains as solid. When pressure is reduced to 1 atmosphere, it sublimes directly to gas.

TEMPERATURE AND PRESSURE TOGETHER:
Both factors determine state:
- High pressure + Low temperature -> encourages liquid or solid state.
- Low pressure + High temperature -> encourages gaseous state.
- LPG: High pressure + cooling -> liquid state (stored in cylinders).
- On releasing LPG from cylinder -> low pressure -> liquid converts to gas (used for cooking).

ATMOSPHERE: atmosphere (atm) is a unit of pressure.
1 atmosphere = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa (Pascal - SI unit of pressure).
Normal atmospheric pressure at sea level = 1 atmosphere.

CONCLUSION: Pressure, along with temperature, determines the state of a substance. By controlling pressure and temperature, we can control the state of any substance.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Evaporation is the phenomenon of change of a liquid into vapours at any temperature BELOW its boiling point. It is a SURFACE phenomenon - only particles at the surface of the liquid that have sufficient kinetic energy escape into the vapour state.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Evaporation occurs at ANY temperature (not just boiling point).
It is a SURFACE phenomenon - only surface particles escape.
BOILING is a bulk phenomenon; EVAPORATION is a surface phenomenon.
At any temperature, particles have different amounts of kinetic energy.
Particles at surface with higher-than-average kinetic energy overcome inter-particle forces and escape.
Evaporation causes COOLING.
The particles that escape have high kinetic energy -> average kinetic energy of remaining liquid decreases -> temperature falls -> cooling.

items.question: What is evaporation? How is it different from boiling?
items.answer:
EVAPORATION: Change of liquid into vapour at any temperature below its boiling point. It is a SURFACE phenomenon - only particles at the surface with sufficient kinetic energy escape.
BOILING: Change of liquid to vapour at the specific boiling point temperature. It is a BULK phenomenon - particles from throughout the bulk of liquid change to vapour.
KEY DIFFERENCE: Evaporation occurs at any temperature (even below boiling point); boiling occurs only at boiling point. In evaporation, only surface particles escape; in boiling, particles from the entire liquid escape.

items.question: Why does a desert cooler cool better on a hot dry day than on a humid day?
items.answer:
On a HOT DRY day:
- Humidity is LOW (less water vapour in air).
- Low humidity allows RAPID evaporation of water from the wet pads/grass in the cooler.
- Rapid evaporation absorbs more heat from the air passing through, cooling it effectively.
On a HUMID day:
- Air already contains much water vapour (high humidity).
- Rate of evaporation from the cooler pads is SLOW (air cannot hold more vapour).
- Slow evaporation means less heat absorption -> less cooling.
Therefore, a desert cooler cools BETTER on a hot dry day due to faster evaporation in low humidity conditions.

items.question: Explain the four factors that affect the rate of evaporation.
items.answer:
Four factors that affect rate of evaporation:

(1) SURFACE AREA:
Larger surface area -> more particles exposed to atmosphere -> more particles can escape -> faster evaporation.
Example: Wet clothes spread on a clothesline dry faster than bundled clothes. We spread clothes to increase surface area for faster drying.

(2) TEMPERATURE:
Higher temperature -> more particles gain sufficient kinetic energy -> more particles can escape from surface -> faster evaporation.
Example: Wet clothes dry faster in summer (high temperature) than in winter.

(3) HUMIDITY:
Humidity = amount of water vapour already present in air. High humidity -> air already contains much vapour -> less capacity to hold more -> slower evaporation. Low humidity -> air can hold more vapour -> faster evaporation.
Example: Clothes take longer to dry on a rainy/humid day.

(4) WIND SPEED:
High wind speed -> water vapour near the surface is carried away quickly -> surface is exposed to fresh unsaturated air -> faster evaporation.
Example: Clothes dry faster on a windy day. Desert cooler works by blowing air over wet pads.

Q5 [4 Marks]: Explain how evaporation causes cooling. Give three examples from everyday life.
A5:
HOW EVAPORATION CAUSES COOLING:

MECHANISM:
At any given temperature, particles of a liquid have different amounts of kinetic energy. Some surface particles have higher-than-average kinetic energy. These high-energy particles overcome the inter-particle forces of attraction and escape from the liquid surface as vapour (evaporation).

When high-energy particles escape:
- Average kinetic energy of the REMAINING liquid particles DECREASES.
- Since temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, the temperature of the liquid FALLS.
- To maintain evaporation, the liquid absorbs heat energy from its surroundings.
- This absorption of energy from the surroundings makes the surroundings COOL.

EVERYDAY EXAMPLES:

EXAMPLE 1 - Acetone (Nail Polish Remover) on Palm:
Acetone is very volatile and evaporates rapidly. When placed on the palm, it absorbs heat energy from the skin to evaporate. The palm loses heat -> we feel COOL. Similarly, spirit/alcohol applied before injection feels cold for the same reason.

EXAMPLE 2 - Earthen Pot (Matka) Keeping Water Cool:
The porous clay of the matka has tiny holes. Water seeps through these pores to the outer surface. This water evaporates from the outer surface of the pot. It absorbs heat from the water inside the pot and from the pot itself. This continuous evaporation keeps the water inside COOL.

EXAMPLE 3 - Sweating Keeps Body Cool:
Our body produces sweat (mostly water) which comes to the skin surface. This sweat evaporates from the skin. During evaporation, it absorbs heat from the body surface. This continuous evaporation of sweat keeps our body temperature from rising - our body stays COOL. Wearing cotton clothes helps because cotton absorbs sweat and exposes it for faster evaporation.

Q6 [6 Marks]: Describe evaporation as a surface phenomenon. Explain why it causes cooling, why we wear cotton clothes in summer, why an earthen pot cools water, and why we see water droplets on the outer surface of a glass containing ice-cold water.
A6:
EVAPORATION - COMPLETE EXPLANATION:

EVAPORATION AS A SURFACE PHENOMENON:
Evaporation is the change of liquid to vapour at any temperature below the boiling point. It is specifically a SURFACE phenomenon because:
- Only particles at the SURFACE of the liquid can escape into vapour.
- Particles in the bulk (interior) of the liquid are surrounded by other particles on all sides, so they cannot escape easily.
- At the surface, particles only have particles below them and to their sides. Surface particles with sufficient kinetic energy can overcome the inter-particle attraction and escape.
- At any given temperature, there is a distribution of kinetic energies among particles. Those at the surface with above-average kinetic energy escape.
This is different from boiling (bulk phenomenon) where particles throughout the liquid gain enough energy and escape from everywhere.

WHY EVAPORATION CAUSES COOLING:
The particles that escape during evaporation are those with HIGHER-THAN-AVERAGE kinetic energy. When these energetic particles leave:
- The average kinetic energy of remaining particles DECREASES.
- Temperature (= measure of average kinetic energy) of the liquid FALLS.
- To continue evaporating, the liquid absorbs heat from its surroundings (or the surface it is on).
- This absorption of heat from surroundings makes the surroundings COOL.
The heat absorbed during evaporation = latent heat of vaporisation (absorbed from surroundings).

WHY WE WEAR COTTON CLOTHES IN SUMMER:
In summer, our body produces more sweat because our body tries to cool itself.
COTTON cloth is a good absorber of water - it readily absorbs sweat from the skin surface.
Cotton exposes the absorbed sweat to the atmosphere (large surface area for evaporation).
The sweat evaporates from the cotton, absorbing heat from the body.
This continuous evaporation of sweat from cotton keeps us COOL and comfortable.
SYNTHETIC fabrics do not absorb sweat - sweat stays on skin making us feel hot and uncomfortable. This is why cotton is preferred in summer.

WHY EARTHEN POT (MATKA) COOLS WATER:
Earthen pots (matkas) are made of porous clay with many tiny pores throughout.
Water from inside slowly seeps through these pores to the outer surface.
This water then EVAPORATES from the outer surface of the pot.
During evaporation, it absorbs heat from the pot and from the water inside.
This continuous evaporation and heat absorption from inside water COOLS the water.
Effect is greater on hot dry days with wind - faster evaporation = more cooling.
This is the principle behind traditional water cooling before refrigerators existed.

WATER DROPLETS ON OUTER SURFACE OF GLASS WITH ICE-COLD WATER:
The air around us always contains some water vapour.
When a glass of ice-cold water is placed in a warm room, the glass surface is COLD.
Water vapour from the surrounding warm air comes in contact with the cold glass surface.
The cold glass absorbs heat from the water vapour -> water vapour LOSES kinetic energy.
When kinetic energy drops below minimum needed to stay as vapour -> water vapour CONDENSES.
It converts from gas (vapour) to liquid (water droplets) on the cold outer surface.
This is CONDENSATION (reverse of evaporation) - gas to liquid change due to cooling.
The water droplets seen on the outside of the glass are from water vapour in air, NOT from the water inside.
This demonstrates: (1) Condensation is the reverse of evaporation. (2) Water vapour is always present in air. (3) Cooling causes condensation.

SUMMARY: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that causes cooling by absorbing heat from surroundings. This principle explains many everyday observations - matka water cooling, cotton clothes comfort, body sweating, condensation on cold surfaces.

EFFECT ON EVAPORATION:
HIGH HUMIDITY: Air already contains a large amount of water vapour. It cannot hold much more. Rate of evaporation DECREASES (slow evaporation). This is why clothes take long to dry on a rainy day.
LOW HUMIDITY: Air contains less water vapour and can hold more. Rate of evaporation INCREASES (fast evaporation). This is why clothes dry quickly on a sunny dry day and why desert coolers work better on dry days.

Q3 [4 Marks]: Explain all four factors affecting evaporation with examples from daily life. How does understanding these factors help us in practical life?
A3:
FOUR FACTORS AFFECTING EVAPORATION:

FACTOR 1 - SURFACE AREA:
More surface area exposed to atmosphere -> more particles can escape -> faster evaporation.
Daily Life Example: When we wash clothes, we SPREAD them on a clothesline rather than keeping them in a bundle. Spreading increases the surface area exposed to air, allowing faster evaporation of water from the clothes -> faster drying.
Practical Use: Farmers spread harvested grain in the sun to dry. Papad is spread on the terrace to dry. All use the principle of increased surface area.

FACTOR 2 - TEMPERATURE:
Higher temperature -> more particles gain sufficient kinetic energy to overcome inter-particle forces -> more particles escape from surface -> faster evaporation.
Daily Life Example: Wet clothes dry FASTER in summer (high temperature) than in winter (low temperature). A hot day after rainfall quickly evaporates puddles from roads.
Practical Use: Clothes dryers use heat to speed up evaporation. Farmers dry crops in hot sun for faster drying.

FACTOR 3 - HUMIDITY:
Air can hold only a limited amount of water vapour at a given temperature. Higher humidity = less capacity for more vapour.
Daily Life Example: On a RAINY DAY (high humidity), clothes take much longer to dry. On a DRY SUNNY DAY (low humidity), clothes dry quickly.
Practical Use: Desert coolers work better in dry/low humidity areas (like Rajasthan) than in coastal humid areas (like Mumbai). Grain must be dried to low humidity before storage to prevent fungal growth.

FACTOR 4 - WIND SPEED:
Wind carries away water vapour from the surface quickly. Fresh dry air replaces it, maintaining a low local humidity near the evaporating surface -> faster evaporation.
Daily Life Example: On a WINDY DAY, clothes dry faster than on a calm day. A ceiling fan speeds up drying of wet surfaces.
Practical Use: Wind mills in coastal and hilly areas. Desert coolers blow air over wet pads. Hair dryers blow hot air to speed evaporation.

PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE: By controlling these factors, we can control the rate of evaporation. To dry things faster: increase surface area, increase temperature, decrease humidity, increase wind speed. Refrigerators work by maintaining low temperature and sealed environment (controlling humidity and temperature) to prevent evaporation and spoilage of food.

items.question: Explain the mechanism by which evaporation causes cooling.
items.answer:
MECHANISM OF EVAPORATIVE COOLING:

STEP 1 - Distribution of Kinetic Energy:
At any given temperature, particles of a liquid do not all have the same kinetic energy. There is a distribution - some particles have higher-than-average kinetic energy, some have lower-than-average.

STEP 2 - Escape of High-Energy Particles:
Particles at the surface of the liquid that have HIGHER-THAN-AVERAGE kinetic energy can overcome the inter-particle forces of attraction. These high-energy particles escape from the surface into the vapour state (evaporation).

STEP 3 - Decrease in Average Kinetic Energy:
When high-energy particles escape, the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles DECREASES. Since temperature is directly related to average kinetic energy, the temperature of the liquid FALLS.

STEP 4 - Absorption of Heat from Surroundings:
To continue evaporating, the liquid needs energy. It absorbs this energy (in the form of heat = latent heat of vaporisation) from its immediate surroundings (the surface the liquid is on, the air around it, the body if sweat evaporates).

STEP 5 - Cooling of Surroundings:
This absorption of heat from surroundings reduces the thermal energy of surroundings -> surroundings become COOL.

CONCLUSION: Evaporation causes cooling because: (a) high-energy particles escape -> liquid temperature falls, (b) liquid absorbs heat from surroundings -> surroundings cool.

items.question: Explain why water kept in an earthen pot (matka) becomes cool. What property of water and the pot makes this possible?
items.answer:
EARTHEN POT (MATKA) - COOLING MECHANISM:

PROPERTY OF EARTHEN POT:
Earthen pots (matkas) are made of porous clay. This clay has thousands of tiny pores (holes) throughout its walls. These pores are large enough for water to seep through but small enough to prevent water from gushing out.

PROPERTY OF WATER:
Water has a HIGH LATENT HEAT OF VAPORISATION. This means it absorbs a large amount of heat energy when it evaporates. This makes water an effective cooling medium.

COOLING MECHANISM - STEP BY STEP:
Step 1: Water stored inside the pot slowly SEEPS through the tiny pores in the clay to the outer surface.
Step 2: A thin film of water forms on the outer surface of the pot.
Step 3: This water on the outer surface is exposed to the atmosphere and EVAPORATES.
Step 4: To evaporate, this water needs energy = LATENT HEAT OF VAPORISATION.
Step 5: This heat energy is absorbed from the water inside the pot and from the pot itself.
Step 6: The water inside the pot loses heat -> its temperature FALLS -> water inside becomes COOL.

FACTORS THAT ENHANCE COOLING:
- Hot dry day: Higher temperature and lower humidity -> faster evaporation -> more cooling.
- Windy conditions: Wind speeds up evaporation -> more cooling.
- This is why matka water is coolest on hot dry days.

SIGNIFICANCE: This is the principle of evaporative cooling. The matka is an ancient, low-cost, eco-friendly method of cooling water without electricity. It uses the physical principles of evaporation and latent heat to maintain cool water temperature.

items.question: Why do we wear cotton clothes in summer? How does this demonstrate the cooling effect of evaporation?
items.answer:
COTTON CLOTHES IN SUMMER - EVAPORATIVE COOLING:

WHY WE SWEAT IN SUMMER:
During summer, environmental temperature is high. Our body temperature tends to rise. The body has a natural cooling mechanism - it produces SWEAT (mostly water) through sweat glands in the skin. This sweat comes to the skin surface.

HOW SWEATING COOLS THE BODY:
Sweat on the skin surface EVAPORATES. During evaporation, sweat absorbs the latent heat of vaporisation from the body surface (skin). This heat absorbed from the body reduces the body temperature. Continuous sweating and evaporation keeps the body temperature within normal range (about 37degrees C in humans).

WHY COTTON IS BEST FOR SUMMER:
COTTON properties that help:
(1) ABSORBENCY: Cotton is a good absorber of water. It readily absorbs sweat from the skin surface.
(2) SURFACE AREA: Cotton fabric has a fibrous structure with many tiny surface areas. It spreads the absorbed sweat over a large surface area.
(3) EXPOSURE: Cotton holds sweat near the skin surface and exposes it to the atmosphere for faster evaporation.
Result: Sweat evaporates quickly from cotton -> more heat absorbed from body -> more cooling -> we feel comfortable.

WHY SYNTHETIC FABRICS ARE NOT GOOD IN SUMMER:
Synthetic fabrics (nylon, polyester) DO NOT absorb sweat well. The sweat stays on the skin surface with limited surface area for evaporation. This makes us feel hot, sticky, and uncomfortable.

DEMONSTRATION OF EVAPORATIVE COOLING: The entire process of cotton clothes keeping us cool in summer is a real-life demonstration of evaporative cooling - evaporation (of sweat from cotton) absorbs heat (from body) and causes cooling (of body temperature).

items.question: Describe five phenomena from daily life that demonstrate the cooling effect of evaporation. For each, explain the mechanism involved.
items.answer:
FIVE PHENOMENA DEMONSTRATING COOLING BY EVAPORATION:

PHENOMENON 1 - ACETONE/PERFUME ON PALM:
Observation: Applying acetone (nail polish remover) or perfume on the palm causes the palm to feel cool.
Mechanism: These are volatile liquids - they evaporate very rapidly. Particles of acetone/perfume absorb kinetic energy from the palm skin particles. They gain sufficient energy to overcome inter-particle forces and escape as vapour. This absorption of heat from the palm surface reduces the thermal energy of skin -> palm feels COOL. Spirit applied before injection works the same way.

PHENOMENON 2 - SWEATING KEEPS BODY COOL:
Observation: On a hot day, our body sweats. After sweating, we feel cool (especially when there is a breeze).
Mechanism: Body produces sweat (water) through sweat glands. Sweat reaches skin surface. High-energy sweat particles evaporate from skin surface. They absorb latent heat of vaporisation from the skin. Skin temperature falls -> body temperature is maintained. Wind/breeze speeds up evaporation -> more cooling. This is why we feel cooler in a breeze when sweating.

PHENOMENON 3 - EARTHEN POT (MATKA) COOLING WATER:
Observation: Water stored in an earthen pot (matka) becomes significantly cooler than the surrounding temperature.
Mechanism: Porous clay walls allow water to seep to outer surface. This water evaporates from the outer surface. To evaporate, it absorbs the large latent heat of vaporisation from the water inside the pot. Water inside loses heat -> temperature falls -> water becomes cool. More effective on hot dry windy days (faster evaporation).

PHENOMENON 4 - SPRINKLING WATER ON HOT ROOF/GROUND:
Observation: After a hot sunny day, people sprinkle water on roofs or open ground to cool them. The surfaces become noticeably cooler.
Mechanism: Water sprinkled on the hot surface evaporates rapidly. The large latent heat of vaporisation of water means it absorbs a large amount of heat from the hot surface. The surface loses this heat and becomes noticeably COOLER. Water has a very high latent heat of vaporisation, making it very effective in cooling hot surfaces.

PHENOMENON 5 - DESERT COOLER:
Observation: A desert cooler effectively cools air in hot dry climates, lowering room temperature.
Mechanism: A fan in the cooler blows air over water-soaked pads (wet grass/fibrous material). The moving air (wind) causes rapid evaporation of water from the wet pads. This evaporation absorbs heat from the incoming hot air (latent heat of vaporisation). The air loses heat -> air is COOLED. This cooled air is blown into the room. More effective on hot DRY days (low humidity = faster evaporation = more cooling). Less effective on humid days.

BONUS - WATER DROPLETS ON COLD GLASS (Reverse Effect):
Observation: Water droplets form on the OUTSIDE of a glass containing ice-cold water.
Mechanism: Warm air around us contains water vapour. Water vapour touches the cold glass surface -> loses energy to the cold glass (cooling of vapour) -> kinetic energy falls below minimum needed to stay as vapour -> CONDENSES (gas -> liquid) on cold surface as droplets. This is CONDENSATION - the REVERSE of evaporation. Instead of liquid absorbing heat from surroundings (cooling effect), here the glass absorbs heat from vapour (condensation). The droplets are from air moisture, not from inside the glass.

OVERALL CONCLUSION: Evaporative cooling is a universal phenomenon. It is used in natural body cooling (sweating), traditional water cooling (matka), modern air cooling (desert cooler), and many other applications. The fundamental mechanism is always the same: evaporation absorbs latent heat from surroundings, causing cooling.

items.question: Evaporation causes cooling because:

options.B: High-energy particles escape during evaporation, reducing average kinetic energy and causing the liquid to absorb heat from surroundings

items.explanation: High-energy particles escape during evaporation. Average kinetic energy of remaining liquid falls (temperature falls). Liquid absorbs latent heat from surroundings to continue evaporation. This absorption of heat makes surroundings cool.

items.question: An earthen pot (matka) keeps water cool because:

options.B: Water seeps through pores and evaporates from outer surface, absorbing heat from water inside
options.C: Air inside the pot is cold
options.D: Clay reacts with water to produce cold

items.explanation: Water seeps through the porous clay to the outer surface. Evaporation from the outer surface absorbs the large latent heat of vaporisation from the water inside, cooling it. More effective on hot dry windy days.

items.question: We wear cotton clothes in summer and not synthetic clothes because:

options.C: Cotton absorbs sweat and exposes it to atmosphere for evaporation, cooling the body; synthetic fabrics don't absorb sweat

items.explanation: Cotton absorbs sweat (good absorbency) and exposes it over large surface area for evaporation. Evaporation of sweat absorbs heat from body, keeping us cool. Synthetic fabrics don't absorb sweat, so less evaporation occurs and we feel hot and uncomfortable.

items.question: Water droplets form on the outer surface of a glass of cold water. This is because:

options.B: Ice inside produces water that comes outside
options.C: Water vapour in warm surrounding air condenses (gas->liquid) on the cold glass surface
options.D: Cold glass attracts water molecules from air

items.explanation: Warm air around the glass contains water vapour. The vapour touches the cold glass surface, loses energy, and condenses (gas->liquid) forming water droplets on the outer surface. The water is from the surrounding air, not from inside. This is condensation - reverse of evaporation.

items.question: After a hot sunny day, sprinkling water on the roof cools it significantly. The most accurate reason is:

options.A: Water is cold so it cools the roof
options.B: Water has a very high latent heat of vaporisation; when it evaporates from the hot roof, it absorbs a large amount of heat from the roof surface, cooling it significantly
options.D: Water wets the roof which is cooler

items.explanation: Water's latent heat of vaporisation is approximately 2260 J/g - very high. When sprinkled water evaporates from the hot roof, it absorbs this large amount of heat from the roof surface. This significant heat absorption causes the roof surface to cool noticeably. The high latent heat makes water particularly effective at cooling hot surfaces.
